samples.summary: Server-supplied document id is cast, not validated, then interpolated unencoded into the next request path
samples.evidence: The delta hardens the error-body path in these three orchestrators (`upstreamErrorJson` at docs/import.ts:195/212, notes/import.ts:~180, slides/import.ts:~236) but leaves the success path next to it trusting the same untrusted body: `const newId = (created.data as { id?: string } | null)?.id` (docs/import.ts:198, notes/import.ts:189, slides/import.ts:241). The only check is truthiness, so a hostile or compromised server (or an HTTP endpoint reached via a `--server`/profile override — `DEFAULT_SERVER` is https but nothing enforces the scheme, config.ts:7) can return `{"id":"../../../../auth/refresh"}` (or any non-string value). `newId` is then interpolated raw into the URL at http-client.ts:289 (`/documents/${docId}/content`, no `encodeURIComponent`, unlike `downloadFileDocument` at http-client.ts:254), so `fetch` normalises the traversal and the CLI PUTs the document body — with the `Authorization: Bearer …` header attached — to a server-chosen path. Impact is bounded (the attacker is the origin that already holds the token), which is why this is minor rather than major, but it is the exact 'a cast is not a check at a network boundary' rule the accompanying lessons doc states, applied one line away from the lines this delta rewrote.

samples.summary: Verbatim forwarding of an upstream error body validates only `error.code`; `message` and all sibling fields are untrusted server content echoed to an agent-consumed stderr
samples.evidence: `upstreamErrorJson` (formatter.ts:127) returns `JSON.stringify(res.data)` for the whole body once `isErrorEnvelope` sees a string `error.code` (formatter.ts:76-85). Nothing constrains `error.message`, extra keys, or size, and the documented consumer of this stream is an LLM agent branching on the code (README 'Errors', packages/cli/skills/docs-import-docx.md:84). A malicious/compromised server, or an operator-pointed `--server`, can therefore place arbitrary attacker-authored text (including prompt-injection content) into the agent's context via `error.message` on any failed import/upload/download, and can also impersonate client-side codes such as `SESSION_EXPIRED` (http-client.ts:157-164) to steer a re-auth flow. Control characters are neutralised by `JSON.stringify` so this is not terminal-escape injection, and the delta narrows rather than widens what is forwarded (it previously printed every body verbatim), so I could not raise this to a concrete exploit — hence low confidence. Hardening would be to forward only `code`/`message` (truncated) rather than the whole body.
